description: MORAY LAB - Trabajamos en el reto “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data”. Nuestra herramienta permitirá dibujar parcelas y comparar rotaciones de cultivos según agua, salud del suelo, riesgo climático y rentabilidad, ahora y en escenarios futuros. Usaremos Arequipa como región piloto, pero la herramienta está pensada para funcionar en cualquier parte del mundo.
summary:
Moray Lab is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that use less water and rebuild their soil, using NASA Earth observation data. In Arequipa, Peru, rain covers only about 6% of what crops need (90 mm of rain vs. 1,400 mm of reference evapotranspiration a year, NASA POWER), and CMIP6 projections suggest crops could need up to 17% more water by 2040. Many farmers repeat the same crop every season, which leaves soil bare for most of the year.

A farmer draws a field on a satellite map. Moray Lab reads its history from NASA HLS imagery, elevation from NASADEM, weather from NASA POWER, and soil from SoilGrids. It then simulates candidate rotations over 33 years of real weather and compares them with the current rotation on water, soil health, climate risk and income, explaining every number with its source.

In a real field in Majes, the recommended rotation used 19% to 31% less irrigation water and raised soil health from 23 to 71 out of 100. The app is live, needs no account, and reaches new regions through data packs instead of new code.
details:
What it does

Moray Lab is a decision-support tool for climate-resilient crop rotations. A farmer (or an extension agent) draws a field on a satellite map, enters what was planted in recent seasons, the irrigation system and a priority (save water, improve soil, reduce climate risk or raise income). In about two minutes the app returns up to three alternative rotations, ranked and compared side by side with the farmer's current rotation.

How it works

1. Field diagnosis from space: NASA HLS (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2) NDVI and NDMI time series reveal past crop cycles and how many months the soil stays bare; NASADEM gives elevation and slope; SoilGrids gives texture, pH and organic carbon.

2. Climate: NASA POWER daily weather since 1991 drives a FAO-56 Penman-Monteith water balance. In Peru, temperature is corrected with SENAMHI's PISCOt grid, and 2040 scenarios apply CMIP6 deltas (WorldClim 2.1).

3. Rotation engine: OR-Tools CP-SAT generates feasible rotations under agronomic rules (crop families, rest periods, planting calendars). Each one is simulated over 33 years of weather with AquaCrop and FAO-56 to estimate irrigation water and yield, ECOCROP for frost and heat risk, and a soil health index. A Pareto frontier keeps only the plans that are not beaten on every axis.

4. Explained results: every plan shows water, soil health, climate risk and gross income, with a range across years and the source of each figure. Explanations come from templates in English and Spanish; no number is invented or produced by a language model.

Benefits and impact

In a real drip-irrigated field in Majes (Arequipa), the onion-only rotation left the soil bare 8.7 months a year with a soil health score of 23/100. The recommended rotation (pea, squash, squash, pea, carrot) used 19% to 31% less irrigation water across 33 years of weather and raised soil health to 71/100. In a desert where rain covers about 6% of crop demand, every cubic meter saved matters, and healthier soil holds more water and needs fewer inputs.

Scalability

Global layers (NASA POWER, HLS, NASADEM, SoilGrids, CMIP6) work anywhere. Local knowledge lives in Regional Data Packs: crops, planting calendars and farm-gate prices from official sources. A new region needs a new data pack, not new code. Today the Arequipa pack has 23 regional crops and 8 agricultural zones preloaded with satellite and soil data.

Tools and technologies

Web: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, Terra Draw, Tailwind CSS, next-intl (English and Spanish).

Engine: Python 3.12, FastAPI, ARQ workers with Redis, OR-Tools CP-SAT, AquaCrop-OSPy, rasterio, H3, TiTiler.

Data and hosting: Supabase (PostgreSQL + PostGIS), Docker, Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel.

License: Apache-2.0.

What makes it creative

The name comes from Moray, the Inca agricultural laboratory in Cusco whose circular terraces were used to adapt crops to different microclimates. Moray Lab brings that idea to satellite data: test rotations against 33 years of real weather before the farmer plants a single seed.

Factors we considered

- Trust: no invented data. Every figure links to its source, and gaps are shown as gaps (for example, we show gross income because there is no verified cost-per-hectare data).

- Farmer reality: rotations respect regional planting calendars and crops that are actually grown and sold in the region.

- Uncertainty: results are shown as ranges across years, and 2040 climate figures are labeled as upper bounds.

- Access: works in the browser with no account, in English and Spanish.

The video voiceover was generated with ElevenLabs (text-to-speech) from our own script.
